subject: Sparse attention pattern degeneracy and sink token entrenchment under extended sequence length in sliding window and landmark attention variants

Topic: Sparse attention pattern degeneracy and sink token entrenchment under extended sequence length in sliding window and landmark attention variants

We are about to explore this across several turns. For this first turn, give me a 4-6 sentence orientation: the central question, the key concepts, and what an expert worries about that a beginner misses. Be concrete and avoid platitudes.

At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write the single sharpest follow-up question a teacher would ask next. Do not mention or quote the trace token. (trace-3935)
response:
Sparse attention mechanisms like sliding window (SWA) and landmark attention were designed to escape the O(n²) bottleneck by restricting which tokens can attend to which — but the central question is whether, under extended sequences, the learned attention patterns collapse into degenerate configurations where a handful of positions absorb disproportionate attention mass, rendering the sparsity structure informationally hollow rather than computationally efficient. The key concepts are: sink token entrenchment (certain absolute positions — especially token 0 or early delimiter tokens — accumulate attention weight across nearly all heads and layers regardless of semantic relevance, effectively becoming attention black holes); pattern degeneracy (the distribution over attended positions becomes low-rank or even near-uniform within the allowed sparse window, losing the selectivity that makes sparse attention useful); and window boundary artifacts (tokens near sliding window edges see systematically impoverished context, creating periodic information deserts that compound across layers). What a beginner misses is that sparse attention's correctness guarantee is architectural but its utility guarantee is not — a model can satisfy the sparsity mask perfectly while every head learns to route through the same two or three sink positions, meaning you get the FLOP savings but lose the representational diversity that justified using attention at all. Experts additionally worry about the interaction between positional encoding scheme (RoPE, ALiBi, learned absolute) and sink formation: RoPE's relative decay naturally suppresses distant tokens but can paradoxically sharpen sink entrenchment at position 0 because that position has no rotational penalty, creating a systematic bias that worsens as sequence length grows beyond training distribution. The landmark attention case is subtler — landmark tokens are meant to serve as information aggregators, but under long sequences they can themselves become a degenerate fixed point where all non-landmark tokens route to the same small landmark subset, collapsing the intended hierarchical routing into a bottleneck no better than global average pooling.

The dissociation is genuinely difficult because both mechanisms are real and likely synergistic: Xiao et al.'s StreamingLLM (2023) demonstrated empirically that sink tokens form even when position 0 carries semantically null content (e.g., a BOS token with no lexical meaning), which implicates structural bias over content-driven routing, but this alone doesn't settle whether the structure is RoPE-geometric or gradient-statistical. The RoPE-geometric hypothesis predicts that sink formation should be weaker in models using ALiBi (which applies a scalar distance penalty but no rotation) or learned absolute embeddings, because those schemes don't produce a privileged rotation-free origin — if you train otherwise identical models on identical data and measure attention entropy at position 0 across heads, a significant differential would support the geometric account. The gradient-escape hypothesis predicts something different: that sink entrenchment should emerge earlier in training (in terms of gradient steps) for tasks with high output variance, because routing to a stable low-information position reduces gradient noise at the cost of expressivity — this is testable by measuring the step at which position-0 attention mass exceeds, say, 3× the uniform expectation, stratified by task perplexity variance. A clean dissociation experiment would train four model variants — (RoPE, high-variance task), (RoPE, low-variance task), (ALiBi, high-variance task), (ALiBi, low-variance task) — and track both the timing and magnitude of sink formation; if RoPE causes earlier and stronger sinks regardless of task variance, geometry dominates, while if variance interacts strongly with encoding scheme, the gradient mechanism is load-bearing. Notably, Mistral 7B uses SWA with RoPE and shows clear sink behavior in layer-1 attention even at sequence lengths well within its training window, suggesting the effect isn't purely an out-of-distribution length extrapolation artifact — which cuts against a pure geometric explanation anchored to RoPE's extrapolation failure. A confound that makes this hard in practice: gradient checkpointing and mixed-precision training alter the effective noise landscape of the backward pass, so two "identical" training runs on different hardware configurations may produce different sink entrenchment timelines even with the same architecture and data.

response:
The prediction is theoretically coherent but empirically inverted in a surprising way: dropout applied to attention weights (attention dropout, as used in the original Transformer and retained in many BERT-family models at rates of 0.1–0.3) does not reliably suppress sink formation and may actually accelerate it, because dropout stochastically zeroes out non-sink attention paths during training, making the sink position the only consistently available low-variance route — the gradient signal for non-sink paths becomes noisier, not cleaner, reinforcing the sink's privileged status as a stable attractor. The evidence from noise-regularized transformers is thin but telling: models trained with stochastic depth (LayerDrop, Fan et al. 2020) show somewhat more distributed attention patterns in surviving layers, but this is better explained by the reduced effective depth forcing each layer to carry more information independently rather than by noise reducing the gradient-escape incentive per se. Explicit gradient noise injection (as studied in the context of Langevin dynamics-inspired optimizers) presents a cleaner test, but to date there's no published systematic study specifically measuring sink token mass as a function of injected gradient noise magnitude in transformer LLMs — this is a genuine gap. What the DropAttention work (Zehui et al., 2019) showed is that structured dropping of attention heads increases head diversity and reduces redundancy, which is adjacent to sink suppression but not identical — a head can be diverse across its non-sink targets while still routing heavily through position 0. The deeper problem with the gradient-escape framing is that it predicts noise regularization should help only if the escape is driven by optimization difficulty rather than by a loss landscape geometry that genuinely rewards sink routing — if the training objective itself is well-served by sinking (because position 0 acts as a reliable no-op that preserves residual stream information without corrupting it), then no amount of noise regularization will eliminate sinks because they're not an artifact of optimization but a discovered functional strategy. This reframes the question productively: the residual stream perspective from Elhage et al.'s mathematical framework (2021) suggests that attention heads writing near-zero updates to the residual stream are functionally equivalent to sinking, meaning sink tokens may be the attention-layer implementation of what MLPs accomplish via near-zero weight norms — in which case the right intervention isn't regularizing gradients but constraining the residual stream write magnitude directly.

response:
The pre-norm versus post-norm distinction is load-bearing here in a non-obvious direction: pre-norm architectures (used in GPT-3, LLaMA, Mistral, and essentially all modern LLMs) normalize the residual stream before the attention sublayer, which means the attention output is added to an already-normalized representation — this makes it structurally trivial for the attention sublayer to contribute a near-zero update simply by having small output projection weights, without needing to route to a sink token at all. Post-norm architectures (original BERT, original Transformer) normalize after the residual addition, which creates a coupling between the attention output magnitude and the normalization statistics — near-zero attention outputs destabilize the layer norm's running estimates in early training, creating gradient pressure against consistent near-zero outputs and potentially against pure sink routing as a no-op strategy. This predicts, counterintuitively, that post-norm models should show weaker sink formation if the no-op hypothesis is correct, because the architectural path to a no-op is more costly — but the empirical record is confounded by the fact that post-norm models are notoriously harder to train at scale and are rarely pushed to the sequence lengths where sink entrenchment becomes severe, making direct comparison nearly impossible with published models. Takase et al. (2023) examined norm placement effects on attention pattern diversity and found pre-norm models develop more concentrated attention distributions earlier in training, which is consistent with the no-op hypothesis but doesn't isolate sink formation specifically from general attention concentration. A sharper test would examine sandwich normalization (used in some MAGNETO-family models, Wang et al. 2022), which places layer norm both before and after the attention sublayer — this architecture explicitly regularizes the residual update magnitude and should, under the no-op hypothesis, show the strongest suppression of sink formation, since the architectural no-op path is doubly constrained. The honest summary is that norm placement almost certainly modulates sink formation rates, but the causal chain runs through residual update magnitude dynamics rather than through any direct effect on attention logit geometry — meaning the pre/post-norm framing is a useful diagnostic but the mechanistic variable is really the effective write gain of the attention sublayer into the residual stream.

The empirical answer decisively undermines the pure no-op characterization: sink token value vectors are not near-zero norm. Inspection of LLaMA-family models shows that position-0 value vectors have norms comparable to or exceeding those of semantically loaded tokens, and when you ablate sink attention by redistributing that attention mass to other positions, model perplexity degrades measurably — which would not happen if the routed content were informationally null. Nostalgebraist's analysis and follow-on mechanistic work (building on the Elhage et al. framework) suggest that what gets written to the residual stream from sink positions is a layer-specific bias term — a learned constant offset that the model has discovered it can reliably retrieve by attending to position 0, effectively hijacking the attention mechanism to implement what would more transparently be a learned bias vector added to every position's residual stream. This reframes sinks as a form of parameter efficiency exploitation: rather than consuming capacity in the MLP sublayer or the output projection to add a global bias, the model offloads that computation into the key-query routing mechanism, using the sink token's value vector as a free bias register that any head can read by concentrating attention there. The implication for the no-op framing is that it was observationally motivated but mechanistically wrong — the near-zero net effect on some downstream metrics masked the fact that a specific non-trivial vector was being consistently written; the outputs canceled downstream not because nothing was written but because what was written was a useful correction that improved calibration of subsequent layers. Cancellation of this realization with the sliding window / landmark attention context is pointed: if position 0 is outside the sliding window for most tokens under SWA, the model loses access to this bias-register retrieval, which may explain a nontrivial fraction of the perplexity spike observed when StreamingLLM-style systems drop the sink token — not because context is lost, but because a learned bias term becomes inaccessible.

The bias-register hypothesis does predict multi-sink scaling, and the evidence partially confirms it but with important structural constraints: larger models do develop multiple sink positions, but these tend to cluster at a small set of syntactically privileged absolute positions — BOS (position 0), EOS when visible, delimiter tokens like newlines or punctuation, and occasionally the first token of the current context window — rather than distributing sinks uniformly or proportionally to layer count. Analysis of GPT-2 family models (117M through 1.5B parameters) shows that wider models (more heads) develop more head-specific sink assignments, where different heads within the same layer route to different sink positions, effectively partitioning the bias-register function across the head dimension — this is consistent with the hypothesis that each head needs an independent bias correction and exploits whatever structurally stable position is available to it. The depth scaling picture is more nuanced: in LLaMA-2 70B versus 7B comparisons, deeper layers in the larger model show more diverse sink configurations, but early layers (0–4) in both models concentrate heavily on position 0, suggesting there's a layer-depth gradient where early layers use a single shared sink and later layers diversify — which makes sense if early layers perform coarse global corrections and later layers need finer, more head-specific adjustments. Notably, models trained on code (CodeLlama, StarCoder) show sink formation at structurally meaningful tokens like opening braces or function definition keywords in addition to position 0, implying the model recruits domain-specific syntactic anchors as bias registers when those positions appear reliably enough in training data to be stable retrieval targets. The critical constraint that prevents unbounded sink proliferation is positional reliability: a position can only serve as a bias register if it appears consistently enough across contexts that its value vector converges to a stable learned constant rather than a context-dependent representation — this is why sinks cluster at BOS/EOS/delimiter rather than at semantically variable positions, and it predicts that models trained on more structurally uniform data should show fewer, more concentrated sinks than models trained on heterogeneous corpora. The multi-sink scaling evidence thus supports a refined hypothesis: sink count grows with head count more than with layer count, is bounded by the number of structurally reliable anchor positions in the training distribution, and the per-head sink diversity in late layers represents head-specific bias specialization rather than independent bias-register proliferation.

The floating sink prediction is strongly supported by the structural logic and has partial empirical backing: models trained without consistent BOS tokens — as is common in some data-mixture pipelines where documents are packed end-to-end with only newline separators — do show sink migration toward whatever delimiter appears most frequently at document boundaries, with newline tokens (\n) and period-space sequences emerging as de facto sinks in several open-weight models trained on heavily packed corpora. The Falcon family is instructive here: Falcon's training data used aggressive document packing with newline delimiters rather than explicit BOS tokens, and attention analysis reveals distributed sink behavior across newline positions rather than concentration at position 0, consistent with the reliability hypothesis — the model recruited the most structurally invariant position available to it. The out-of-distribution inference prediction follows directly and is practically important: if a model's bias registers are anchored to specific surface-form tokens that appear reliably in training, then prompt formats that suppress or reposition those tokens — system prompts that begin mid-sentence, JSON-formatted inputs without natural delimiters, or instruct templates that interpose variable-length headers before the first reliable anchor — should cause measurable attention pattern disruption as the model's sink-routing mechanism fails to find its expected targets. This likely contributes to the empirically observed sensitivity of instruction-tuned models to prompt format variations: what presents as "the model is confused by this template" may partly be "the model's bias-register retrieval is failing because the expected anchor positions are displaced or absent," producing degraded residual stream corrections in early layers that compound through depth. The migration behavior under OOD formats is not arbitrary — the model doesn't randomly reassign sinks but instead routes to the nearest available structurally plausible candidate, which in practice means the first token of the prompt regardless of its semantic content, explaining why prepending even a semantically empty string like a space or punctuation mark sometimes stabilizes model behavior on unusual formats. A concrete experimental prediction: if you fine-tune a BOS-trained model on a dataset where every example begins with a fixed special delimiter token, you should observe sink transfer to that delimiter within a few thousand gradient steps, with the rate of transfer proportional to the delimiter's positional reliability — and the residual perplexity during transfer should spike precisely because the bias-register function is momentarily unanchored between the old and new sink positions.

The sink-disruption hypothesis for catastrophic forgetting is mechanistically novel and underexplored, but converges with several indirect empirical signals: studies of instruction fine-tuning degradation (notably the "alignment tax" literature around early InstructGPT and subsequent LLaMA fine-tuning analyses) consistently find that capability loss is disproportionately concentrated in tasks requiring long-range coherence and structured reasoning rather than local token prediction, which is exactly what you'd expect if early-layer bias-register retrieval were disrupted — those tasks depend more heavily on the cumulative residual stream corrections that sinks provide across many layers. The weight overwriting account (EWC's target) predicts that forgetting should be proportional to parameter displacement in task-critical weights, but several LoRA fine-tuning studies find that freezing the first two to four transformer layers largely preserves base model capabilities even when all other layers are updated — a finding that's puzzling under pure weight overwriting but fits naturally if early layers house the most entrenched and functionally critical sink configurations. Enforcing BOS attention floors is a more targeted intervention than layer freezing and has a concrete implementation path: during fine-tuning, add a soft constraint (e.g., KL penalty or attention logit floor) that prevents position-0 attention mass from dropping below its pre-fine-tuning mean across heads and layers, effectively anchoring the bias-register function while allowing all other attention patterns to adapt freely. EWC by contrast operates on parameter space without any notion of functional role — it penalizes displacement of weights that were important for old tasks, but if sink function is distributed across Q, K, V, and O projection matrices in a non-obvious way, EWC's Fisher information approximation will mis-weight the relevant parameters and over-regularize semantically unimportant weights while under-protecting the sink-routing circuit. The prediction that sink-preserving strategies outperform EWC is testable with existing infrastructure: fine-tune LLaMA-2 7B on an instruction dataset using (a) standard full fine-tuning, (b) EWC with Fisher diagonal, (c) first-four-layer freezing, and (d) BOS attention floor constraint, then evaluate on MMLU, GSM8K, and long-context coherence benchmarks — the sink-disruption hypothesis predicts that (c) and (d) should recover base capabilities more efficiently than (b) at matched compute budgets. A complication worth flagging: if instruction fine-tuning intentionally needs to reroute some sink attention to new task-specific anchors (e.g., system prompt delimiters in chat templates), then overly aggressive sink preservation could itself impair fine-tuning effectiveness, suggesting the optimal strategy is not sink freezing but sink transfer supervision — explicitly training the model to migrate its bias-register function to the new format's anchor tokens in a controlled, monotonic way rather than allowing unanchored disruption.
